title: The Phishing Message
description: You receive a suspicious message asking for your bank OTP. Explore your digital rights and duties under India's Information Technology Act, 2000.

begin.text: You get a text message claiming to be from your bank, asking you to click a link and enter your OTP to 'verify your account'. What do you do first?

choices.text: Do not click the link. Check the sender and contact your bank directly through its official number.
choices.feedback: Good instinct. Under Section 66D of the IT Act, cheating by personation using a computer resource -- like a fake bank message -- is a punishable offence. Verifying independently protects you from it.

choices.text: Click the link and enter the OTP since it looks urgent.
choices.feedback: Sharing an OTP this way can lead to identity theft, which Section 66C of the IT Act specifically penalises -- but prevention is safer than any legal remedy after the fact.

bad_choice.text: Entering the OTP allowed someone to access your account without authorisation -- an offence under Section 43 and Section 66 of the IT Act. Let's see how you can respond now.

choices.text: Learn from this and start again with a safer first move.
choices.feedback: Recognising the mistake quickly is the right instinct -- the next node covers how to report it.

consider_reporting.text: You suspect the message was a phishing attempt. What's the right way to report it?

choices.text: Report it on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in) or call the 1930 helpline.
choices.feedback: Correct. India's Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In), set up under Section 70B of the IT Act, coordinates the national response to exactly this kind of incident.

choices.text: Delete the message and don't report it, since no money was lost.
choices.feedback: Reporting unsuccessful attempts still helps -- it feeds into national cyber-threat intelligence, even when you personally weren't harmed.

data_rights.text: A few weeks later, a company you'd shared personal data with suffers a data breach through negligence on their part. What right protects you here?

choices.text: You can claim compensation, since the company was negligent in protecting your data.
choices.feedback: Correct. Section 43A of the IT Act makes a body corporate liable to pay compensation if it negligently fails to maintain reasonable security practices for sensitive personal data it holds.

choices.text: Nothing can be done since you agreed to their terms and conditions.
choices.feedback: Agreeing to terms of service doesn't remove a company's legal duty to protect your data with reasonable security practices under Section 43A.

finish.text: Scenario complete. Digital rights come with digital responsibilities: verify before you trust, report what you can't verify, and know that Indian law -- via the IT Act, 2000 -- gives you real recourse against identity theft, phishing, and data negligence.
